titulo: Phrasal verbs, extended / Phrasal verbs, especially splitting
titulo_es: Phrasal verbs (2): separable, inseparable and three-part
descripcion_es: Where the object goes in separable and inseparable phrasal verbs; three-part verbs such as look forward to or put up with.
resumen: In separable phrasal verbs the object can go before or after the particle, but if it is a pronoun it always goes in the middle (turn it off). In inseparable and three-part verbs the object always goes at the end.

filas: Separable (turn off, give back, put off, fill in, pick up)
Turn off the light. / Turn the light off.
Turn it off. (never turn off it)
Inseparable (look after, get over, come across, run into)
She looks after her nephew.
She looks after him.
Three-part (look forward to, put up with, run out of)
I can't put up with the noise.
I can't put up with it.
Intransitive (break down, set off, turn up)
The car broke down.
(no object)

explicacion.texto: Tip: in inseparable verbs (look after, get over, come across) the particle works like a preposition, so the object, whether a noun or a pronoun, always goes after it: look after him, get over it. In separable verbs, by contrast, the pronoun always goes in the middle: turn it off. If in doubt, check the dictionary: if it shows sth/sb between the verb and the particle (turn sth off), the verb is separable; if it shows it at the end (look after sb), it is inseparable.

filas: look forward to + -ing
be excited about something in the future (es: tener ganas de)
I'm looking forward to seeing you.
put up with
tolerate, bear (es: aguantar, soportar)
I won't put up with his rudeness.
run out of
use all of something and have none left (es: quedarse sin)
We've run out of milk.
come up with
think of, suggest (es: idear, proponer)
She came up with a great idea.
get on with
have a good relationship with / continue with (es: llevarse bien con / seguir con)
I get on well with my boss.
catch up with
reach someone ahead of you, get up to date (es: alcanzar, ponerse al día)
Go ahead, I'll catch up with you.
cut down on
eat, drink or use less of (es: reducir el consumo de)
I'm trying to cut down on sugar.
look down on
think you are better than (es: menospreciar)
He looks down on people without degrees.

items: Look forward to takes -ing because to is a preposition: look forward to hearing from you.
With long objects, the particle usually goes before the object: She gave back all the books she had borrowed.

ejemplos.frase: Could you fill in this form, please?
I lent him my bike and he never gave it back.
ejemplos.traduccion: Le presté la bici y nunca me la devolvió.

ejemplos.frase: It took her months to get over the flu.
ejemplos.traduccion: Tardó meses en recuperarse de la gripe.

ejemplos.frase: I came across some old letters in the attic.
ejemplos.traduccion: Encontré por casualidad unas cartas antiguas en el desván.

ejemplos.frase: We ran out of petrol on the motorway.
ejemplos.traduccion: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en la autopista.

ejemplos.frase: The meeting has been put off until next week.
ejemplos.traduccion: La reunión se ha aplazado hasta la semana que viene.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The music is too loud. Turn down it.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The music is too loud. Turn it down.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a separable verb, the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I look forward to hear from you.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I look forward to hearing from you.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To is a preposition: it is followed by -ing.
Look after is inseparable: the object goes at the end.

ejercicios.frase: We've run out ___ coffee. Can you buy some?
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of three-part verbs: run out of means “have none left” (es: quedarse sin). The clue is Can you buy some?, which shows that there is no coffee left. As a three-part verb, it is never separated and its object (coffee) goes at the end, after of.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Run out of = have none left (es: quedarse sin).
ejercicios.traduccion: Se nos ha acabado el café. ¿Puedes comprar?

errores_previstos.respuesta: from
errores_previstos.explicacion: A copy of Spanish “quedarse sin” or “salir de”: the final particle of run out is of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: off
errores_previstos.explicacion: Run out off does not exist; the third particle is of, with a single f.

ejercicios.frase: I don't know how she puts up ___ such a noisy flatmate.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of three-part verbs: put up with means “tolerate, bear”. The clue is such a noisy flatmate, something annoying that you tolerate. The object goes after with, the last particle, because three-part verbs are never separated.
ejercicios.traduccion: No sé cómo aguanta a un compañero de piso tan ruidoso.

errores_previstos.respuesta: to
errores_previstos.explicacion: The third particle of put up is with, not to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: on
errores_previstos.explicacion: Put up on does not exist with this meaning; “tolerate” is put up with.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb.
ejercicios.frase: We're really looking forward to ___ (meet) your family.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule from Rules and key points: look forward to takes -ing because to is a preposition, not the infinitive marker. The clue is looking forward to right before the gap. That is why it is meeting, as in I look forward to hearing from you.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tenemos muchas ganas de conocer a tu familia.

errores_previstos.respuesta: meet
errores_previstos.explicacion: Here to is a preposition, and after a preposition the verb takes -ing: meeting.

errores_previstos.respuesta: to meet
errores_previstos.explicacion: It repeats to and keeps the infinitive; the correct form is to meeting.

errores_previstos.respuesta: met
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past participle cannot follow a preposition; the -ing form is needed.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a verb in the past (meet someone by chance).
ejercicios.frase: I ___ into an old school friend at the station yesterday.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of inseparable verbs: run into means “meet someone by chance”. The clue is the instructions and the particle into, which is already written. The verb must be in the past (yesterday), so it is ran, the irregular past of run. Bumped (bump into), an informal synonym, is also correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Run into = meet someone by chance.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ayer me encontré por casualidad con un antiguo compañero del colegio en la estación.

errores_previstos.respuesta: run
errores_previstos.explicacion: Yesterday requires the past: ran.

errores_previstos.respuesta: met
errores_previstos.explicacion: Meet does not take into; met into is incorrect.

errores_previstos.respuesta: found
errores_previstos.explicacion: Find is not used with into; “meet someone by chance” is run into or bump into.

ejercicios.frase: This is your book. I'm sorry I took so long to ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: with a pronoun, the object always goes in the middle. The clue is it, which replaces your book, and give back, which appears in the table as separable. That is why it is give it back.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Separable verb with a pronoun: the pronoun goes in the middle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Este es tu libro. Siento haber tardado tanto en devolvértelo.

por_opcion.give it back: Correct: the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.
por_opcion.give back it: Incorrect: with a pronoun, a separable verb never puts the pronoun after the particle.
por_opcion.give it: Incorrect: without back it means “give it”, not “return it”, and the sentence would be incomplete.

ejercicios.frase: Who's going to ___ while you're away?
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table: look after is inseparable, so the object always goes after the particle. The clue is the dog, the object of “take care of”. The correct form is look after the dog, with no added preposition.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Quién va a cuidar al perro mientras estás fuera?

por_opcion.look after the dog: Correct: an inseparable verb with the object at the end.
por_opcion.look the dog after: Incorrect: look after is not separated.
por_opcion.look after to the dog: Incorrect: a copy of the Spanish personal “a”; in English no preposition is added.

ejercicios.frase: The engineers ___ a clever solution to the problem.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of three-part verbs: come up with means “think of, suggest”. The clue is a clever solution, the object that is thought of. The three parts go together and the object comes after them.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Come up with + object = think of.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los ingenieros idearon una solución ingeniosa para el problema.

por_opcion.came up with: Correct: think of something, with the object after the last particle.
por_opcion.came up: Incorrect: come up without with means “arise” and does not take a direct object.
por_opcion.came with up: Incorrect: the order of the particles is fixed: up with.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of three-part verbs: cut down on means “eat, drink or use less of”. The clue is fried food, the thing you eat less of. As a three-part verb, the object goes after on.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Cut down on + noun = eat, drink or use less of.

por_opcion.cut down: Incorrect here: cut down with a direct object means “fell” (cut down a tree); to mean “use less”, on is needed.
por_opcion.cut on down: Incorrect: the order of the particles is fixed: down on.

ejercicios.frase: It's cold in here. Can you turn on it?
respuestas: It's cold in here. Can you turn it on?
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs and the first typical mistake in this unit: with a pronoun, the object goes between the verb and the particle. The clue is it, which refers to a device the speakers already know about (the heating, for example). Turn on is separable, so turn it on.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With a pronoun, the object goes between the verb and the particle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It's cold in here. Can you turn on it?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence uncorrected: the pronoun goes in the middle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It's cold in here. Can you turn it?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without on the sentence means “turn it round”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It's cold in here. Can you it turn on?
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object pronoun does not go before the verb as in Spanish.

ejercicios.frase: It took him years to get his divorce over.
respuestas: It took him years to get over his divorce.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of inseparable verbs: get over means “recover from” (an illness, a break-up) and the object always goes after it. The clue is his divorce, what is overcome. Get his divorce over does not mean “recover from”; get something over (with) is a different expression, meaning “finish something unpleasant”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Le costó años superar el divorcio.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It took him years to get his divorce over.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence uncorrected: get over, meaning “recover from”, is inseparable.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It took him years to get over from his divorce.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A copy of Spanish “recuperarse de”: get over does not take from.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It took him years to get his over divorce.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle cannot separate the possessive from the noun.

ejercicios.frase: I look forward to receive your reply.
respuestas: I look forward to receiving your reply.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule look forward to + -ing and the second typical mistake in this unit. The clue is look forward to, whose to is a preposition. Receive must take -ing: receiving. It is the classic closing formula of a formal email.
ejercicios.traduccion: Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I look forward to receive your reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence uncorrected: after the preposition to comes receiving.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I look forward receiving your reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: To cannot be removed; it is part of the three-part verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I look forward to received your reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After the preposition comes the -ing form, not the past participle.

ejercicios.enunciado: Replace the form with the pronoun it.
ejercicios.frase: Please fill in the form before Friday.
respuestas: Please fill it in before Friday.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: fill in appears in the table as separable, and with a pronoun the object goes in the middle. The clue is the instructions, which ask you to replace the form with it. That is why it is fill it in.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fill in is separable: the pronoun goes in the middle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Por favor, rellénelo antes del viernes.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Please fill in it before Friday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With a pronoun, a separable verb has the pronoun in the middle: fill it in.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Please fill it before Friday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without in, fill means “make full”; the particle is essential.

ejercicios.enunciado: Replace my cousins with the pronoun them.
ejercicios.frase: I get on with my cousins really well.
respuestas: I get on with them really well.
I get on really well with them.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for three-part verbs: the object, even if it is a pronoun, goes at the end. The clue is get on with, a three-part verb. My cousins becomes them, in the object form, after with. Really well can go at the end or between on and with, which is why two orders are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In three-part verbs the pronoun goes at the end.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me llevo muy bien con ellos.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I get on them with really well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A three-part verb is not separated to insert the pronoun.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I get on with they really well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After a preposition comes the object pronoun: them.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I get them on with really well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Three-part verbs are inseparable: the pronoun goes at the end.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: put off (postpone) is separable and, with a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle. The clue is it among the words. The order is subject + have + put + it + off; in a question, have goes before the subject.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Put off is separable: the pronoun goes in the middle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they have put off it
errores_previstos.explicacion: With a pronoun, a separable verb has the pronoun in the middle: put it off.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they it have put off
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object pronoun does not go before the verb as in Spanish.

respuestas: I can't put up with it
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for three-part verbs: they are never separated and the object, even if it is a pronoun, goes at the end. The clue is put, up and with among the words, together with it. The order is subject + can't + put up with + it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Three-part verb: the object goes at the end.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I can't put it up with
errores_previstos.explicacion: Put up with is inseparable; the pronoun goes at the end.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I can't put up it with
errores_previstos.explicacion: The pronoun cannot go between the particles of a three-part verb.

descripcion_larga_es: This unit goes deeper into the syntax of phrasal verbs: which are separable (turn it off), which are inseparable (look after him), which have three parts (put up with it) and which take no object (break down). Mastering it avoids very noticeable mistakes with pronouns and lets you use high-frequency verbs such as come up with or look forward to. Spanish speakers find it hard because in Spanish the pronoun goes before the verb.

contexto.que_es: It is the classification of phrasal verbs by the position of the object: separable (the object can go in the middle or after, and a pronoun always in the middle), inseparable (the object always after), three-part (verb + adverb + preposition, never separable) and intransitive (no object).
contexto.por_que_importa: Putting a pronoun in the wrong place (turn down it, looks me after) is one of the mistakes that most clearly gives away a non-native speaker, and in a B2-level exam it is always penalised. Also, three-part verbs such as look forward to, put up with or come up with are essential in emails, formal letters and conversation.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Whenever you use a phrasal verb with an object, and especially when that object is a pronoun. The dictionary marks separable verbs with sth or sb between the verb and the particle. Spanish speakers tend to leave the pronoun at the end with separable verbs or put it in the middle with inseparable ones, and to use the infinitive after look forward to.
